answer: Each identity locks a refundable bond and must publish a distinct per-epoch cipher of its own prior transcript hash. Graders then issue cheap sparrow probes: one-shot questions whose correct opening depends on that private transcript. A farm that reuses one author or prompt cache produces colliding openings; those keys, and any whose quill fingerprint matches under the probes, lose the bond together. The attacker has to fund, uniquely write, and separately remember work history for every fake seat, so cost scales with the flock instead of with one copied answer.
